cells.tense: The care in your hands right now comes from your own choosing, and you carry it as yours.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you're keeping going and one small act of care for it, then do the act and let the note stand as the record.
cells.core:
An ordinary day here looks like water poured, a check-in made, a small adjustment done because it was needed, and then you moving on to the next thing. You give what's growing the conditions it needs and you don't rush it past its own pace. You can tell when to step in and when to leave it alone, and that judgment is the skill — it's the one you lean on most, and it's why the things you tend tend to last.

The strength underneath isn't gritted teeth; it's hope that's kept its footing through plenty of ordinary mornings, and it shows in how you show up without announcing it. What this steadiness can carry next: turn some of that same care toward the one giving it. Name whose work it is, once, where you can hear yourself say it.
cells.sheetLine: You keep it growing without gripping it.
cells.verb: still keeping faith with the thing you chose

cells.tense: You're already a few steps into a tomorrow that hasn't arrived, bracing for what it will ask of you.
cells.ask: Pick one growing thing and leave it untouched for a full day — no check, no adjustment, nothing.
cells.core:
On a good day you give what's growing what it needs and then you let it be. You notice the water, the light, the small move that helps, and you don't add anything on top. The care is steady and it doesn't crowd, and things develop under it at the pace they were going to take anyway. That patience is the whole of it.

Lately the care is running several steps ahead of the thing itself — pre-deciding, pre-worrying, pre-solving — at a pace you're setting rather than the one it's on. The hurry is chasing an outcome it can't force, and it's costing the thing its own timing. Let one matter sit for a day. What opens is room to see what it actually needs from where it is.
cells.sheetLine: You're pushing what you're growing past the pace it can hold.
cells.verb: still keeping faith with the thing you chose

cells.tense: You're standing at a door that's already closed behind you, looking at ground you've stopped tending.
cells.ask: Do one small concrete thing for something in front of you — water it, contact them, finish one step.
cells.core:
On a good day you do the small plain thing a growing thing needs — you water it, you ask how it's going, you take one step — and you don't watch it while it happens. You know how to give conditions and step back, and you know it works because you've seen it work before. Small acts, done steadily, are enough for the thing in front of you.

There's a patch nearby that's gone quiet and you've stopped expecting anything from it. The doing itself has run down, so the simplest move feels heavier than it is. One small act for something that's actually here is the way back. Care that doesn't wear you out refills itself in the doing, not before it.
cells.sheetLine: You've been tending the gone-quiet patch from a distance.
cells.verb: still keeping faith with the thing you chose

cells.tense: You're already keeping conditions together for something or someone, and you talk about it as though the situation were doing that on its own.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, 'I keep this going,' about one thing you look after, and then keep looking after it.
cells.core:
On a good day what you carry is visible to you — you know when you've made it easier for something to keep going, and you take that in stride. You adjust, you check, you give what's needed, and you count it as yours. That accounting is quiet, but it's what lets the strength stay with you instead of drifting off into the situation.

The acts are running now, but the credit goes to the job, the person, the circumstances — nowhere you can collect it. The strength feels borrowed instead of kept, which is what makes it easy to underrate. Claim one thing as yours. Holding without forcing is the older, simpler shape of it, and one thing named out loud puts it back in your hands.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding something together and giving the credit elsewhere.
cells.verb: still keeping faith with the thing you chose

The asks are ordinary acts with a finish — picking one planted thing and leaving it alone, waiting a day before a next step, doing one tending act without standing over it, doing one thing by hand — and all four survive being wrong about the person, because each one teaches something either way.
